analysis.one_liner: Strips the tax deduction from employee pay above 25 times a company's lowest-paid worker's salary.
analysis.headline: The bill to end tax deductions for pay above 25 times a company's lowest wage never got a hearing or a vote in the 113th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The Income Equity Act of 2013 would have changed the tax code so that a company could no longer deduct as a business expense any employee's compensation above the greater of 25 times what its lowest-paid full-time worker earns or $500,000. All forms of pay would count — salary, bonuses, stock options, retirement contributions — and companies with such pay gaps would have to report their pay ratios to the Treasury. The idea: if shareholders and taxpayers effectively stop subsidizing outsized pay packages, companies have a reason to either raise wages at the bottom or trim pay at the top.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the change would mainly benefit employees at companies with wide pay gaps: firms would have a tax reason to either raise the lowest wages (raising the 25x cap) or reduce top pay. Ordinary taxpayers would also gain indirectly, because corporate deductions for outsized pay packages are currently a subsidy that broad-based taxpayers effectively underwrite. Companies that already keep top pay within 25 times their lowest wage, or under $500,000, would be untouched.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at companies with wide pay gaps

how_it_helps.text: It would deny businesses a federal tax deduction for any employee's pay above the greater of 25 times their lowest-paid worker's pay or $500,000, meaning companies would pay tax on that excess rather than deducting it like an ordinary business expense.
It would cover every form of pay — salary, bonuses, stock options, retirement contributions, deferred compensation — so total packages, not just base salary, would count.

It would require companies with such pay gaps to file a public report showing their lowest-paid worker's pay, average non-managerial pay, average executive pay, and the exact pay of their top five employees, making pay ratios visible.
By making excessive pay a partially taxable corporate expense, it would give companies a direct financial reason to either raise bottom wages (widening the ratio limit) or trim top pay.

analysis.who_pays: Companies (mostly large ones) whose top employees earn more than 25 times their lowest-paid worker's pay — or more than $500,000 — would pay more in taxes on that excess compensation. Their executives and the compensation consultants who structure pay packages would face reduced incentives to build large packages and new public reporting of top pay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large firms and their top executives

drawbacks.text: The 25-to-1 ratio is measured against the single lowest-paid full-time employee, so a large company with many minimum-wage workers would face the tax penalty even if its executives were paid far below $500,000 in total compensation.

A $500,000 annual pay cap on deductibility is low relative to typical pay packages for executives of large public companies, and critics would argue it could push compensation into harder-to-trace forms or make it harder for American firms to compete for executives internationally.
The bill was never debated or amended in committee, so there was no opportunity to fix design problems or weigh the objections above.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its merits, the bill would have used the tax code to discourage the widest gaps between executive and worker pay, with the strongest objection being the risk that rigid 25-to-1 caps would penalize large firms with tens of thousands of low-wage workers even when their top pay is moderate in dollar terms. A fairer benchmark could be designed, but the bill never received a hearing, so its design was never tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never scheduled a hearing or a vote, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Lee introduced the Income Equity Act of 2013 on January 4, 2013, the first week of the new Congress.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which controls all tax legislation.
That referral was the bill's last action of record — no hearing, no markup, no vote for the entire two-year Congress.
Only four House members, all Democrats, signed on as cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies paying executives multiples of their workers' wages kept an intact tax deduction for that pay, since the bill never advanced. No House committee or floor vote was ever held.

for.name: Rep. Barbara Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 4, 2013 and assigned it to the Ways and Means Committee.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 4, 2013 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the 113th Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House agenda and the Ways and Means Committee's calendar; no tax bill without committee approval reaches the floor, and none was scheduled for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors were Democrats; the House was under Republican control and the bill never received any hearing or vote.

industries.industry: Large corporations with high pay gaps between executives and workers
industries.note: They would lose the tax deduction for any compensation above the greater of 25 times their lowest-paid worker's pay or $500,000, raising their federal taxes unless they narrowed pay gaps. Because compensation includes bonuses, options, and retirement contributions, the cap would reach most of a typical executive package.

Pay above the threshold would no longer be a deductible corporate expense, and the bill would require their companies to report the exact compensation of the top five employees, adding public scrutiny to executive pay.
New ratio limits and reporting requirements would create work restructuring executive packages, though the bill never advanced far enough for this to materialize.
